utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, ladies and gentlemen, the technical booth, the interpreters, the legal officers, court reporters, Ms. Kirsten. Good morning, Mr. Harmon, Mr. McCloskey, Mr. Cayley. Good morning, Ms. Holmes. Good morning, Mr. Petrusic, Mr. Visnjic. Good morning, General Krstic. We're going to continue our case. Today, Mr. Butler, you're going to answer questions which the Defence counsel has for you, and I remind you that you are still under oath. Mr. Petrusic, finally it's your turn. Your witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] First of all, may I say good morning, Mr. President, Your Honours, my learned friends from the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Butler. Mr. Butler, the cross-examination by the Defence, as already established with the Prosecution early on, will be based on your report which you produced on the 5th of April and the 15th of May. In your report, dated 5 April, in a brief historical survey, you said that the army of Republika Srpska was formed from the remnants of the former Yugoslav People's Army, so I should like to ask you to explain this concept of the remnants of the former JNA and I would add with a question, was that the only element from which the army of Republika Srpska was formed?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: In reviewing the documents that we seized from the VRS, particularly those pertaining to the early years, they discuss the issue of the fact that the army of Republika Srpska was -- or essentially evolved from those units that remained behind when the remainder of the Yugoslav National Army withdrew in May of 1992. So in that sense, the embryo of the army came from those military formations. We also understand -- I also understand from reading that material that many of the territorial organisation based units that were there were wrapped into the army as it was formed and it became a formal structure. As the months progressed through mid and later 1992, elements of what we traditionally call the paramilitary units, those units that were operating outside of a lawful command and control of either the army or the party at the time, many of those units by presidential decree were either folded into the army and placed under illegitimate command or they were disbanded. So in that respect, that is my understanding of how the initial nucleus of the army formed, the elements that folded into the army of Republika Srpska through mid-1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: And the army of Republika Srpska was a constitutional category, was it not?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The army of Republika Srpska was a legally formed entity by the Republika Srpska constitution and its rules and regulations were codified in both the defence law and the law on the army, yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: The doctrine of the army of Republika Srpska, did it differ from the doctrine of the former JNA?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: My analysis of the doctrine as it evolved from 1992, when the VRS formed out of the remnants of the JNA in Bosnia, through 1995 indicates that there were no major substantive changes with regard to command and control and organisational structure. Now, clearly there were probably a number of minor changes that occurred as a result of the learned experience from combat in the prior three years.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: One of the elements of that doctrine were the combat operations assigned to certain military units. The combat operations engaged in by the army of Republika Srpska, as part of its doctrine, were they defensive and static as opposed to the JNA which, in its doctrine, envisaged as its main principles offensive combat operations?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The JNA doctrine as I understand it, while it discusses the offence as a significant doctrine, gives just as much attention to other aspects of the doctrine as well to include defensive operations and particularly to include the conduct of military operations in occupied territory. So in that regard, I would not say that the JNA-based doctrine is weighed in favour of the offensive. In reviewing the army of Republika Srpska operations, while it is fair to say that as a whole the army reflected the political goals, which was a strategic defence, after the Republika Srpska had achieved the majority of the territorial gains which it desired by the end of 1992, certainly at the corps and brigade level, offensive operations were conducted in a variety of situations depending on the tactical situation or operational situation on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Mr. Butler, in the documents seized from units of the army of Republika Srpska, were the regulations from August 1992, I think -- so my question is, did those regulations apply to the 4th Corps of the former JNA?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 4th Corps JNA documents, those particular regulations, were not part of seized material. They were part of documents that were provided to us by the BiH government which they gained custody of when the JNA left Sarajevo in 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: The Drina Corps, was it established in the area of responsibility of the 4th Corps of the former JNA?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: To my knowledge, only a small segment of that, which would include the 2nd Romanija Brigade and some elements near Gorazde would have been included in the area of the former 4th Corps of the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Is it possible to deny the assertion, bearing in mind this fact that you have just referred to, that the Drina Corps did not act according to the rules for the 4th Corps of the former JNA?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not believe I ever made the assertion that the 4th Corps JNA rules were specifically applicable to the Drina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Mr. Butler, I put this question to you because in the footnotes of your April report, reference is made to the regulations of the corps of the ground troops, number 4, referring to the 4th Corps of the former JNA, and that was the reason for my question.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I recall that footnote, sir, the idea that I was trying to bring forward was the fact that the 4th Corps JNA regulations at the time represented an excellent example of how a corps would take the base JNA regulatory documents and how they would institutionalise those rules and those series of instructions in order to ensure that they were operating in accordance with the base JNA documents. In that respect, it was my analysis that the 4th Corps document represents an excellent example of how to do that, and further, as the JNA transitioned into the VRS and as the 4th JNA Corps transitioned to become the VRS Sarajevo-Romanija Corps, that that would be an excellent example of how those regulations would still be adhered to.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Every corps of the former JNA had its own regulations, did it not? And those regulations and -- were those regulations of an internal nature, that is, were they applicable to that corps alone?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: My understanding of how the system worked is that the answer is, yes, each corps would have made its own series of internal regulations. They would have been certainly applicable to that corps. As part of that process, those same regulations would have been subject to the review of the parent organisation. In the case of 4th Corps, it would have been the 2nd military district; in the case of the VRS Corps, it would have been the Main Staff of the VRS. The presumption is that an individual corps would not be permitted to publish instructions that were so far out of line from the base documents and regulations that that corps would essentially be operating under an entirely different series of guidelines than the other formations of the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: In the process of transition of the former JNA and the establishment of the army of Republika Srpska which was founded in May 1992, as well as the Drina Corps which was established in December 1992, if this is a well-structured army which respects the constitution and the law on the army, was it essential to have a normative document for the corps to serve as a guideline for its activities?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It would be normal to do that. My understanding is that in fact it was done.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Mr. Butler, let us now move on to a second section, and that is the Commander and the Chief of Staff of a VRS Corps. The Corps Commander, does he realise his function of command directly without any intermediaries?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Corps Commander, by both the regulations and the practical application as demonstrated, commands the corps through the series of intermediaries, as you've used the word, or at least how it's been translated, which, in effect, are his subordinate commanders and staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: There may be a problem in the translation. Does the Corps Commander command directly and without intermediaries, independently without intermediaries?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: He commands through his intermediaries, yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: So his intermediaries, if we can call them that, issue orders to lower-level units.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Commander is the position and function that issues the order; the staff, the intermediaries, are the mechanism by which his instructions are formulated into an order and then passed down to subordinate units. That is my understanding of the documentation, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: To make myself quite clear, an order issued by the Corps Commander to a brigade, is it issued by the Commander, or is it the Chief of Staff who issues that order to the brigade?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Technically, sir, it could be both, or it could be either, depending on the circumstances.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: In your report, paragraph 2.1, you say that the right to control and command units and institutions of the corps is the exclusive responsibility of the Commander; however, your previous answer, as I understand it, negates this statement that you made.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir, that's not a correct interpretation. What I mean to say, depending on the circumstances, and as I also discuss in my report, is that once the Commander issues a broad directive, in many cases the Chief of Staff operating within the guidance and the framework of the Commander is empowered to issue supplemental orders or orders to the lower units, the brigades or the staff, in order to further the Commander's guidance. I don't mean to imply in any way, shape, or form that anyone other than the Commander commands the corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: And the right to issue guidelines within the framework of the orders given by the Corps Commanders, the orders or commands given by the Corps Commanders, what about those?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, within the framework of the orders or the guidance given by the Corps Commander, presumably at the discretion of the Corps Commander, the Chief of Staff, and even Assistant Commanders and other staff officers, can issue orders to the subordinate formations, again, in keeping with the orders and directions of the Commander.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Butler. In fact, you said before it could be either according to the circumstances. So we have to be very clear. "Technically, sir, it could be both, or it could be either, depending on the circumstances." This has to be completely put into form. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: To clarify it for us.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Further on, Mr. Butler, you talk about the concept of unified activities. We're now talking about the Chief of Staff, so the Chief of Staff has a unique role within the structure of the corps. My question is whether this idea of a unique role, is it a legal concept, and whether the rules governing the corps include any such term, as you have used to describe its role as unique?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: As the corps rules articulate, the Chief of Staff, as concurrently the Corps Deputy Commander, is the only person who, other than the Commander, is authorised to pass orders to subordinates. When he's -- as the Chief of Staff is the only other person designated as the Corps Deputy Commander, in that sense he is unique; and under the JNA regulations as adopted, that specific role and responsibility is articulated.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: But regarding his basic activities as Chief of Staff, there is no mention of the fact that he passes on the Commander's orders and that he has this unique role that you referred to. Those duties are listed under ten points.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Going back to the base JNA regulations which I've cited in my report, I believe under the roles and responsibilities of the Chief of Staff, those issues are, in fact, raised; that as the Commander of the staff, a large portion of his function is taking the Commander's guidance and orders and putting it into a format where it can be transmitted down to subordinates. Those are all -- those are all detailed as part of those functions.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Are the directives regarding command part of the regulations of the corps?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The directives pertaining to command are found in the two base JNA documents, the Corps Rules on Peacetime and the Base Corps Rules Provisional. As an example, those provisions of command were articulated in the 4th Corps JNA document which I used as an illustrative point. Within the Drina Corps specifically, as I do not have the Drina Corps instructions during the wartime period, I'm unable to say whether or not those tenets of command are articulated in them.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: According to the rules and regulations of the 4th Corps of the former JNA, the Corps Commander does issue directives.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: From the documents that you had access to during your research work, did you ever come across a document which would point to the fact that the Corps Commander or the Chief of Staff of the corps is authorised, is empowered, to issue directives?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I understood that correctly, sir, what you asked me was, have I come across a document that specifically authorises or empowers a Corps Commander to command his corps. Is that correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: No. My question was: In the material that was available to you, did you -- were you able to reach a conclusion that the Corps Commander was empowered to issue directives in the sense that they are issued by the Supreme Commander and the Main Staff, directives not orders? I'm referring to the directives as an act, that is, within the purview of the Supreme Commander and the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not come across any documents which could indicate that the Corps Commander is authorised to issue instructions for areas or activities that are within the purview of either the Main Staff or the Supreme Command, no, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Can we therefore say that the Corps Commander issues assignments to its subordinate units through orders and commands?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That would be a fair statement, sir. Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Mr. Butler, can we say that as regards the function of the Deputy Commander, there are no special powers of the Deputy Chief of Staff -- Deputy Commander, I'm sorry, except the fact that he can take over the role of a Commander in those circumstances when the Commander is not capable of exercising his function?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would argue that the powers and authority to assume that Commander's role and function in those circumstances in fact qualify as uniquely special powers which only he possesses as the Chief of Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Special powers. But only in the absence of the Commander.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: As was noted in the regulations, it's not just the physical absence of the Commander, it's also under circumstances where the Commander may be unable to effectively exercise command, sir. So it's not just qualified on a physical absence.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: The Commander, therefore, and we are talking about the Corps Commander, can in that case be present in its area of responsibility and have at the same time the Chief of Staff take over the role of the Corps Commander; would that be your interpretation?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can envision a circumstance, for example, the Commander on a portion of the battlefield or for a technical reason, unable to communicate with his staff and where immediate decisions had to be made, where the Chief of Staff, understanding the Commander's temporary absence, would in fact issue the required orders. So certainly the regulations make provisions for those types of exceptional circumstances, yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Those circumstances, are they regulated by the corps regulations or by the law of the army or some other statutory acts or sublaws?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: There are actually within the framework of -- certainly if not law, certainly within the regulations where it is expected that in the absence of orders in an extraordinary circumstance, that the next higher ranking individual would give the required orders. We see at the very lowest levels that idea manifested in the service regulations of the VRS published in 1992, where even at the lowest levels of the army, it is expected that in the absence of orders, should the circumstances dictate, the senior officer or senior person present Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. would issue orders to be taken.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: I'm clear on that, Mr. Butler. However, what I'm interested in is whether in those statutory laws and sublaws there's any provision for the particular circumstances in which that can take place. When I say "circumstances," I refer to certain operations that are being conducted, the unavailability of the Commander, or any other reason for this particular situation to take place.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not believe that any of those more detailed types of guidance are found in any of the base defence laws or laws on the army, sir, no. I believe they're all found only within the relevant military regulations and orders that pertain to the operation of the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: In combat operations, when they do take place, and also in the absence of combat operations, the corps -- the Chief of Staff of the corps is the person who is coordinating the work of the Corps Command; is that true?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, that's a fair statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: I think that we can agree that the Drina Corps, as well as other corps of the VRS, were under the immediate command of the Main Staff of the army of the Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: The Main Staff of the VRS, does it get directives, not orders but directives as a statutory law, from the Supreme Commander?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, Mr. Butler, and I apologise to Your Honours and the President. When I say "directive as a statutory act," I am saying that for the benefit of the interpreters because the directive is very often translated as an order, which is a different act, which refers to an act of command, and I would like to avoid any misunderstanding in this area.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: In that sense, the Main Staff receives its -- the directives and guidance, if you will, from the Supreme Command of the Republika Srpska. That would be the chief agency responsible for ultimately directing the course of the war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Mr. Butler, excuse me, but in answering Mr. Petrusic's questions, he drew our attention to the need to differentiate between the directive and the order of command. But I'm not sure from our end we understand in the way you answer the question what you conceive to be a directive versus an order, and an example would be very helpful.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe the best practical application of an example would be going back to one of our early exhibits which was Republika Srpska Supreme Command Directive 7, which in essence articulated out the broad orders and guidance of the political leadership to be, in turn, executed by the military. The Main Staff takes operation -- Directive 7 and then publishes their version of it, which is Directive 7/1, which takes that guidance and expands upon it for the Corps Commanders. It takes much of that guidance and puts it in the phrases and terms of operational orders for the military unit. So I believe that is what Mr. Petrusic is referring to as the process.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: So ultimately, what is the sanction of disobeying a directive?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Under the laws of the army and the general laws on military service, the disobeying of such directives and orders of that nature qualifies as a punishable offence, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: So both orders and directives are compulsory?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: I think we can clarify this situation in the following manner: The directives are acts which can be issued only by the Supreme Commander of the armed forces of the Republika Srpska and the Main Staff of the VRS. The directives as such cannot be issued by a corps, a brigade, and, of course, by other lower units such as platoons or companies. Would that be correct, Mr. Butler?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe maybe where we're mixing it up is an issue in how the words translate in context. In my view, a directive is a very broad set of guidance. Mandatory guidance, but guidance just the same. An order is a much more specified, much more -- I don't want to say specified directive, but it's a much more specified product. So in a sense, from echelonment of command, I would agree that the Supreme Command level and the Main Staff would issue the broader directives, and the Corps Commanders would issue more specified orders. But at the same time, particularly if you look at operations order 7 or directive 7, some of the guidance in that particular directive is very specific, and is, in fact, literally copied by the Main Staff in its transmission to the corps. So I wouldn't put orders and directives in an apples and oranges type of cart that one level of command can issue and another one can't. And again, maybe that's the way it's coming out in English for my interpretation or my view of the words, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: You said that the disobeyance of directives, specifically in this case you refer to Directive 7, entails sanction, and it is a punishable offence that entails a certain responsibility. In that directive, Directive 7 and 7/1, one of the tasks was that the army of Republika Srpska achieve certain objectives during the year 1995. Those objectives were not reached, and to your knowledge, were any Superior Commanders held responsible for that, for failure to obey the directive, to execute the directive?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's a rather broad channel, but what I would say along that framework was that certainly the army is obligated to attempt to meet the goals of the directive, and if they fail to attempt to meet those goals, they would -- or they could conceivably face sanctions by the President of the Republic. In taking your point further, sir, as the Court and history is aware, on 4 August, President Karadzic did, in fact, attempt to remove General Mladic as a member of the Main Staff for circumstances. In a sense, that could infer the army, or certainly the Chief of the Main Staff in the army, incurring a form of a penalty for failing to meet the object of the directive, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Since you have mentioned it, did he try to punish him or to relieve him from his duty for not entering Tuzla, which was the objective of the directive, or for what happened in Srebrenica; or was that something that had been going on for quite a while between the two of them, that kind of disagreement or conflict?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly my understanding is that by 1995 there was a general disagreement between General Mladic, as the Chief of the Main Staff of the army, and the political leadership as to the conduct of the war. Having said that, I believe it would be speculation on my part if I tried to identify a specific cause as to why President Karadzic tried to relieve General Mladic, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: You stated, Mr. Butler, that the directives were issued by the political leadership, including the Directive 7. That particular directive was signed by the Commander of the armed forces of the Republika Srpska, that is, Radovan Karadzic. So he did not sign it as the President of a political association or a political party, he signed it in his capacity as the Supreme Commander. How can you therefore conclude that this was a directive issued by a political leadership?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: In reviewing the RS laws on the army and defence, it specifically articulates that the President of the republic is also the Supreme Commander of the armed forces. Because of that statement, I base my conclusion on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: The conclusion that it was issued by political leadership.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Mr. Butler, it was not my intention to dwell on the issue of directives for such a long time; however, there are certain things that need to be clarified. Would it not be preferable to say that the leadership was that of a state and not just political leadership, but state leadership, because Mr. Karadzic was the President of the State -- Head of State?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is a correct statement, sir, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: So the directive was issued by the President of the Republic and the Main Staff and it -- when it reaches the corps, does the corps then analyse this directive and does it transform it into an order or a command which, in turn, are subsequently transmitted to lower units as a form of statutory command documents?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: In a broad sense, that is how the process should work, sir, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Does the Chief of Staff issue orders in any other case, except for the case when he is replacing or acting on behalf of the Commander, in the sense that you have mentioned it, for example, due to his absence?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. According to the regulations, the Chief of Staff is also designated as the head of the corps staff and is empowered to issue orders to the subordinate officers of the corps staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Therefore, an order can be issued by him only when he is replacing the Commander or acting for the Commander.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir, that's not what I meant to imply. What I meant to say was that when he is in his role functioning as the Corps Deputy Commander, those circumstances apply. When he is performing the functions, his normal functions as the Corps Chief of Staff, under the regulations he is empowered to issue orders to the corps staff officers who are subordinate to him. The issuing of orders that he does, while in theory within the framework and guidance of the Corps Commander, should not require the Corps Commander's either physical presence or detailed guidance in order to perform the effective functioning of the job, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: His is the role of the Deputy Corps Commander only when the Corps Commander is not there, only when the Corps Commander is absent.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: As the regulations note, it's not just a physical absence, sir. It is other circumstances where the Corps Commander is unable to effectively command. So again I would be hesitant to tie that condition to a physical absence.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: In your previous answer, it was stated that the conditions of a physical absence of the Commander are not provided for in the regulations.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir. What I said was that the provisions for the physical absence of the Commander were not broadly provided for under the defence laws or army laws, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: The Assistant Commander for Security, does he have a dual kind of subordination, the one that's going towards the Corps Commander and the other one towards the Chief of Security Service of the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would not, under the circumstances, use the phrase "dual subordination," which would inadvertently imply a dual chain of command. The Corps Assistant Commander for Security, by the regulations, is subordinate to the Corps Commander. There is, in fact, a chain, a communications link, where technical guidance, where management issues, administrative issues flow to that next higher level, that being the Chief of Security of the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: In his activities and reporting, is the Assistant Commander for Security always obliged to inform the Corps Commander about his activities in all cases?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I noted in previous testimony, my readings of the security regulations note that issue. However, it also -- again, taking into account the specific role of the security officer, in the case where the Corps Commander himself may be the object of the investigation, in that regard certainly the security officer would not inform the Corps Commander of that fact; however, that decision would most probably have been made by the Commander of the superior echelon above that. But for the daily activities of the Security Branch, the Assistant Commander -- Assistant Commander for Security would be informing the Corps Commander of those activities.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: In your report, on page 39, points 8 and 9, you talk about the Chief of Staff and you say that in performing his duties he coordinates the activities of the corps staff and the work of subordinate commands and ensures complete unity of action in relation to directives and the ideas of the Commander.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Notwithstanding different words for translation, the gist of that is in fact correct, sir, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: When speaking about directives, did you mean directives as a legal document issued by the Main Staff and the Supreme Commander, or did you mean a command document issued by the Corps Commander?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this regard, it is a document issued by the Corps Commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Does the Commander or Chief of Staff coordinate the work of subordinate units?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: There are two aspects to look at that question. In a narrow aspect, it would not be the function of the Commander or the Chief of Staff to coordinate the internal activities of a select subordinate unit. In that regard, that is the purview of the subordinate unit Commander and his staff. On a broader perspective, it would be the Corps Commander and corps staff's responsibility to coordinate the activities of multiple subordinate units to ensure that more than one unit, in this case, more than one subordinate unit is acting in concert with each other and towards the goals of the corps order. So within the narrow confines of the unit, no, sir; but within the parameters of coordinating the activities of the subordinate units, yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: You said that the Chief of Staff of the corps is obliged to monitor the ability of units and to submit to the Commander reports on the results of this supervision. The results of subordination, this [indiscernible], does it exist at all within the system of command in the army regardless of the level, be it the corps, lower level units, or the superior command?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I could ask you to repeat, sir. There was a word that didn't come through in translation, and I think it's kind of critical to the question, so if I could ask you to repeat the question, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For the interpreters, it is page 39, paragraph 8.10, third: "The Corps Chief of Staff --"

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay, sir, I understand. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: "The Corps Chief of Staff is required to monitor --" third, "The Corps Chief of Staff is required to monitor the readiness and the ability of subordinate units, to execute the orders of the Commander and to report the results of the compliance back to the Commander." The key word here is this compliance. And my question is whether such a wording, the results of the compliance, can be found in any command or control document at the level of the corps which the Commander transmits to lower echelons, subordinate units, or he may receive such a document from a superior command containing such a wording.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: With respect to the regulations, I believe that the direct literal translation refers to the phrase "and ensures they are carried out," which I then take in English to infer ensures compliance. The practical application of that, and it is as you suggest, sir, endemic through the entire chain of command, the daily and interim combat reports which notify from lower to higher the results of operations for the subordinates for the benefit of the higher command to realise what is occurring, what missions are being accomplished, what missions cannot be accomplished and what the status of them is, so in that sense, it is in fact completely accurate.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: The regular or interim combat reports, periodical or operative reports, and all the other kinds of reports that exist, are they sent to the superior command by the Corps Commander or the Chief of Staff?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: With regard to the corps level reporting echelon, the report is sent out in the name of the Corps Commander to the Main Staff. This is not to mean that on each and every day the Corps Commander authors the report. The responsibility of putting together the report rests within the broad responsibilities of the Chief of Staff; however, in most practical applications, that duty then is further delegated to the duty officer. But at the end of the day, and as articulated in the Main Staff guidance, the Main Staff expects the daily report that it receives to be an accurate reflection of the events in the command, and further, if the Commander's signature is on it, that he is, in effect, validating the accuracy of that report, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Such a report, may it be sent by the Chief of Staff if the Commander is present?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't see any reason why that wouldn't be feasible, sir, no. It would again be up to the individual Commander in question.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Lower level subordinate units, in this case brigades, do they send their regular and interim reports to the Commander, to the Corps Commander?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: As evidenced in the variety of exhibits that have been produced to date, on certainly a minimum of a daily basis, the reports are sent to the Corps Command, yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: We are now referring to paragraph 8.12 in which you say: "That despite his more limited command authority, the Corps Chief of Staff still assumes a significant degree of responsibility pertaining to the commission of illegal acts." You're here obviously making a certain distinction in relation to criminal responsibility. I don't know whether I'm making myself clear. I don't quite understand what the comparison is with when you talk about the degree of responsibility.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the SFRY regulations pertaining to the application of the Rules of International Law of War, there are three broad categories where they define where an officer or soldier can be held liable. One of them, and as previously discussed, is the category of superior responsibility; the second one is the category of individual responsibility; and the third one is the category of individual responsibility for carrying out illegal acts under orders. In the sense of paragraph 8.12, in that regard I am specifically qualifying it as the responsibility for breaches of the Rules of Law of War committed on orders.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: When the Chief of Staff is acting as the Chief of Staff when his Commander is present, does he have to be aware of any violations of the provisions of the law of war, or in other words, are there any circumstances when he may not have any knowledge about it or may not have been informed about it?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Clearly, as you indicated in the question, it would be impossible to make the assumption that just by virtue of the individual being the Chief of Staff that he would be knowledgable of 100 per cent of the activities to occur at a given time, particularly with regard to illegal acts which may have occurred. So I would agree that that's a physical impossibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: The function of Chief of Staff, does it consist primarily of collecting information of an operational nature about the progress and outcome of combat activities, logistics support for those activities, and the like?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those activities that you've discussed are in the spectrum of his responsibilities to collect information about and monitor the activities of, yes, sir. Along the same vein, the other two branches, the morale, legal, and religious service and the security service would also fall within his purview to have to monitor the activities of and be aware of what is happening with those as well. He has responsibility for doing that throughout the entire corps staff, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I would like to suggest we have a break now, but of course I will stand by your decision whether that suggestion is acceptable to you or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Yes. [Interpretation] I think it is a good time for a break. So we are having a 20-minute break now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Petrusic, you may go on.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Mr. Butler, let me now move on to the report about the military events in the area of Srebrenica, that is, the Operation Krivaja 95. Before I begin with specific questions, I just want to note that you probably were given a very specific assignment by the Prosecutor as to the particular area that had to be analysed, but I should like to know whether you think that for the purpose of having an overview of the situation in Srebrenica and all the events that took place at the relevant times, and also before the area was proclaimed as a safe area, during that time and after the fall of Srebrenica, do you think that it would have been a good idea to discuss the period from 1992 until the area was proclaimed as a safe area, though you do deal with that period to a certain extent? So my question is actually: Do you think that that period would also contribute to a general overview of the situation and tell us more about the causes and effects of the events and developments that took place there?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I noted in the introduction to the narrative, and as you so noted, sir, it is a limited scope of analysis with respect to three specific areas. On a broad level, I'm aware of the events that occurred there and occurred in Eastern Bosnia in general from 1992 to 1995 and have included some of them in order, again as you note, to place the issues of July 1995 into context. However, and again, an analytical judgement on my part, I did not feel that a long analysis and review of historical events from 1992 through the beginning of the safe area and from the safe area on would be required in order to analyse the military events that occurred from 1 to 11 July 1995 and the events that occurred subsequent to that, which the analysis represents my trying to link military units and individuals to known crime scenes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: You say that main seat of the Drina Corps was established in Vlasenica. I assume that by that you are referring to the command post of the Drina Corps as being in Vlasenica.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, the headquarters of the Drina Corps in Vlasenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Apart from Srebrenica and Zepa, which were declared safe areas, was a part of the Gorazde safe area also under the responsibility of -- under the area of responsibility of the Drina Corps?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: My understanding is that some units of the Drina Corps held positions along parts of the Gorazde safe area. So with that regard, I make the inference that with at least some territorial area, the Drina Corps had some responsibility for the Gorazde safe area, yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Can we say, therefore, that the forces of the VRS, by making certain plans, by drafting certain plans, had the intention to prevent military activities of the Muslim formations, and I am referring mainly to the 8th Division and the Tactical Group of the Srebrenica safe area, and the intrusion of such forces to the rear area of the Drina Corps units which were deployed along their static positions around the safe area?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The VRS documents that we have indicate that the Bratunac Brigade, the Milici Brigade, and the Skelani Separate Battalion were, in fact, in a static defensive posture around the Srebrenica safe area with the goal of preventing Muslim movement in and out of the safe area, smuggling operations, as well as combat raids.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Those plans, did they have as an objective to prevent the linking of the two enclaves, the Srebrenica and the Zepa enclaves, bearing in mind the fact -- an undisputed fact, if I may say so -- that an area had actually remained between the two enclaves which was not covered by the forces of the Drina Corps, and that there was some unhindered communication between the two enclaves which was used for some smuggling operations but also for purely communication purposes? And is it true that the enemy forces of the Drina Corps were intruding in that area and conducting combat raids against the units of the Drina Corps and the civilian population?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay, sir, there are three questions embedded there. Let me go over them one at a time. As to the first one, did the plans have an objective to prevent the linking of the two enclaves, Srebrenica and Zepa, that is in fact clearly articulated in the plans. Specifically, we see that articulated in both Drina Corps operations -- I'm sorry, the Main Staff Directive 7/1 and the Supreme Command Directive 7 to ensure the physical separation of the enclaves. The second question, my understanding of the VRS documents as we've received does in fact confirm that despite the deployments of the Milici Brigade, the Bratunac Light Infantry Brigade, and the Skelani Separate Battalion, there was, in fact, a gap in the lines which the Muslims used for both communications and smuggling. So in that respect, that's also correct. And that, again, leads to your third question, is it true the enemy forces -- I assume when it says -- translated "enemy forces of the Drina Corps," I assume you're referring to the Muslim military forces, were they operating in that zone and conducting combat raids. Again, the answer is yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Was there any danger, if I may say so, for the forces of the VRS, or specifically the forces of the Drina Corps, for a linking of the two enclaves to take place. First of all, the linking of the Srebrenica and Zepa enclaves, and subsequently the linking with the area of Tuzla, that is, with the forces of the 2nd Corps of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: In that regard, and again, qualifying my expertise as based on the VRS documents and orders that I've read which reflects that situation, again, my analysis reflects what I read in those materials. In that regard, the VRS was extremely concerned about the linking of the Zepa and Srebrenica enclaves. I do not get a reflection, certainly from the 1995 period documents that I possess, that there was such a broad concern that the Muslims in Srebrenica, the 28th Infantry Division at that time, would be able to physically establish a cohesive link, a combat link, with the forces of BiH 2 Corps. Now, having said that, and as previously noted in testimony, there was in fact a relatively active passage between Srebrenica and the forces of BiH 2nd Corps in Tuzla which smugglers and couriers carrying material orders and ammunitions frequented along that line. So while not a physical linkage, certainly a tenuous line of communications existed between the Srebrenica enclave and the Muslim forces in Tuzla, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Mr. Butler, what we have been discussing so far, does that constitute military elements which led the army of the VRS and the Drina Corps forces in certain of their intentions?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe you're referring to -- and if I can rephrase the question just to make sure I understand it accurately: Are the military forces that you're referring to, would they be the Muslim military forces in question?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: No. There has probably been a misunderstanding. Speaking about the intentions of the VRS, about the concerns relating to the Srebrenica and Zepa enclaves, were those elements, those aspects which did exist at the time, that is, the intrusion of the enemy forces into the formations of the army of Republika Srpska and the civilian population, the potential danger of the linking up of the two enclaves, do these things present -- constitute exclusively military aspects, military elements that guided the VRS army in their decisions when it comes to certain military operations and combats at that time?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, they certainly do.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Pursuant to Directive 7 and 7/1 of the Supreme Commander or the Main Staff, were military -- rather, combat operations around the enclave and in the direction of the enclave, were they intended to be very restricted in their scope; that is, was the objective to separate the enclaves and to bring them down within the boundaries -- within the confines of the safe areas in question?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. That intent is pretty clearly articulated in both directives.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: The boundaries of the safe areas which were established pursuant to a resolution of the Security Council issued in May 1993, did they remain fixed, the same, as they had been established by the Security Council, or did those boundaries change during the period of time when the safe area was in place?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The short answer is that I don't know that. I do know from the documents from both the VRS and from the UNPROFOR forces that both the VRS and the BiH were unhappy with the relative boundaries that were established, and there was constant conflict between the two over what the boundaries were, but I am unable to go into any specifics over what issues or why.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Mr. Butler, reading through your findings, I fear that we may lose continuity for the Chamber and the public, but my intention is to refer exclusively to your findings so that I hope the Chamber will have understanding for my method of doing this cross-examination, and of course you as well, Mr. Butler, because we will be referring to it from time to time again. When the military operations in the enclave started on the 6th of July, 1995, were there any activities or combat activities against the United Nations forces, or rather the UNPROFOR, the Dutch Battalion?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The combat activities that occurred with regards to the Dutch Battalion, as described by the Dutch Battalion, were a series of combat activities that in most cases weren't directed against them per se; however, they did receive fire in specific instances, but were designed to put the relative Dutch observation posts in a position where they were untenable and the Dutch would abandon those posts and even move further into their own lines or towards Srebrenica or place themselves in the custody of the army of Republika Srpska. I have no indication from the documents that the army of the Republika Srpska specifically targeted the Dutch as a military target with the specific intent of defeating them on the battlefield in a classic military sense. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry, but I was expecting Judge Riad to make a comment.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: A part of the Dutch Battalion forces, did they surrender to the forces of the VRS, and analysing their statements, did you come to any such conclusion?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe using the phrase "surrender" is, in effect, unfair. The accurate statement that I would use is that given the situation, they placed themselves in the custody of the VRS. In my mind, "surrender" implies defeat or a defeated enemy, and clearly in the case of the Dutch, this was not the case. It was just a case of placing themselves in the safe custody of the army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: So without the use of force or weapons, one could call it a voluntary placing of themselves in the custody of the VRS, that they did so voluntarily, in a sense; of course, on the basis of their assessment of the overall situation regarding individual observation posts?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would agree with that statement up to the point of "without the use of weapons," because clearly there was weapons fire involved as part of the process.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: But not directed against the members of the Dutch Battalion. When they placed themselves under the protection of the VRS?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: In most cases, from the Dutch statements, that's true; however, there are two specific incidents where Dutch witnesses report, and it's reflected in their reports, that they were specifically engaged by the army of Republika Srpska directly. So I would agree with you: In the majority of the cases, that's true. There are still, in fact, specific instances where they were targeted.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Mr. Butler, in the course of your analytical work on this case, and it has taken quite some time, did you acquire any knowledge as to the casualties of the Muslim forces during the operations from the 6th until the 11th of July, 1995? When I say "casualties among the Muslim forces," I'm referring to the population, the Muslim population that was in Srebrenica and around Srebrenica at the time.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The documents that we have pertaining to the situation in the enclave or in Srebrenica proper, that we have from the Muslims' talks about the situation and does talk in broad terms that they are taking casualties. Those casualties, the specific numbers are not delineated. So on a broad sense, yes, the Muslims took casualties, both military and civilian; but I have no way to qualify that in a scheme of numbers, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Apart from being an analyst, you are also a military man, a military officer of the Army of the United States, and in any event, you have a great deal of military experience. So taking into account statements that a large number of shells were fired, up to 200, within a relatively short period of time, so on the basis of your professional experience, would you say that the number of casualties would be enormous if the target had been the column formed in the town of Srebrenica or the town of Srebrenica itself and the surrounding locations inhabited by Muslim population?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: As part of, as you note, being an analyst and having military experience, one of the dangers is when one receives a report, as you've noted here, the large number of shells fired, up to 200, in a relatively short period of time, it's dealing with a general abstract like that. The reports don't qualify whether we're talking about large-calibre shells capable of causing significant damage and casualties, and they don't qualify whether it's a small-calibre shell such as a 30-millimetre anti-aircraft round which, hitting a building, would qualify as a shell impact, but unless it hit a specific person or target, wouldn't have that. So in that respect, I don't want to take a single number and try to extrapolate a large number of casualties. However, along the lines of the regard that you've noted, considering the military dispositions of the VRS and the fact that in many cases they had direct lines of observation to the civilians in the town or the column as -- or the assembly at the UN base Bravo in Srebrenica, had those been the intended target, it's reasonable to assume that they would have suffered significant casualties.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: When the Muslim inhabitants gathered and assembled, their gathering and the decision to abandon the town, did it come about spontaneously, or was it based on a decision taken by a certain leadership, be it a military or a civilian leadership?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I've noted in the narrative, my understanding of the chain of events that occurred is that sometime on the late evening of 10 July, the Muslim leadership in Srebrenica made the decision to abandon the town. I believe it was a combined military-civilian decision that did that, but because of the lack of data, I can't be 100 per cent sure of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: On the basis of the documents available to you, is it possible to infer or was it possible for you to conclude that the population of Srebrenica was the target of combat operations? Was the population of Srebrenica the target of combat operations?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have never made the contention that the civilians of Srebrenica were the target of the operations. I do not believe that, and I have no evidence from the VRS which indicates that in the actual military takeover of the town of Srebrenica, that civilians represented the target.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: The group of several thousand, and data differ, ranging from 10.000 to 15.000 that had assembled in Jaglici and Susnjari, was that group armed?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I believe I've noted earlier, that is in fact -- the column is a mixed military and civilian group. There were many soldiers, perhaps up to 1.000, who were part of that column and who were armed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: You're referring to the column that numbered 10.000 to 15.000 civilians and military men.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: The column that is moving from Jaglici and Susnjari.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: The indictment upheld by my learned friend Mr. Harmon, we find the fact that one-third of that column was armed. We hear from you today that about 1.000 members of that same group, 1.000 of the Muslim fighters, were under arms.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: My understanding of the composition of the column reflects that one-third of the column were military members or potential military members; the remaining two-thirds were not. I don't believe, considering the state of weapons that the 28th Division at the time had, that we could make the case that 5.000 people in that column were, in fact, armed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Excuse me. What do you call potential military members?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 28th Infantry Division had a large number of members on its rosters, at least, the rosters that we have from the early 1995 time frame. Again, their consideration of the eligible military population pool were those military members between the age of 15 and 65. In many aspects, because they didn't have enough weapons, these people were technically considered part of the military but were not actually in and present in formations. One of the customary practices that used to occur within the scope of the Muslims while they were in the enclave is the fact that unarmed soldiers would come up to the lines, take the weapon of the soldier who was going off-duty, and they would use that weapon during their period of duty. So it's within that framework where I qualify it as potential military members.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: So does that mean that they were armed?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Most of the members of the 28th Division as organised in Srebrenica did not -- were not under arms. They qualified as members of the military, as members of the military organisation, but because of a lack of weapons, they were not armed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Mr. Butler, on the basis of which data are you saying that there were about 1.000 armed combatants?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The two pieces of information or two bodies of information that I used to make that determination are the various witness and survivor accounts from people who trekked as part of the column, and also the information and understanding of the army of the Republika Srpska in their own intelligence reporting about the column.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Intelligence information of the army of Republika Srpska about the armed members of the column refer to the 13th and 14th of July, that is, when the column had partially been broken up, when it was entering the area of Mount Udrc and is trying to make a breakthrough towards Nezuk, Nezuk and Bajkovica, when it is split into three different directions. And intelligence information of the Zvornik Brigade come from several sources.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe the first intelligence report on the column originates from the early morning hours of 12 July as based off of intercepted communications from local commanders who are along the Nova Kasaba-Konjevic Polje-Milici road. In that regard, they are referring to the column earlier, and certainly we see other written reporting coming out on the evening hours of the 12th July to the Drina Corps pertaining to their estimates of the column. So there's two separate series of reporting, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Mr. Butler, I have here a book entitled "Crafty Strategy," Sefer Halilovic, the Commander in Chief of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. I will not tender it into evidence in this part of the trial, but I would like to show you a report by Mr. Halilovic who says that the strength --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Excuse me. I'm going to have to object at this point, Mr. President. If there are documents or reference materials that were going to be used by the Defence to cross-examine Mr. Butler, the Prosecution believes it's entitled to at least see copies of those at the time that they are being used to question the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Petrusic, what is your response to this objection?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I withdraw the question, and I will continue with the cross-examination. I will withdraw the intention to show this text to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, if that's counsel's wish. We don't wish to, obviously, infringe on his right to cross-examine. We would just like to be able to see what he is using to cross-examine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Surely the parties always have the right to put any questions, so long as they are relevant and put properly. So I think that we have a problem here. It is possible to quote a sentence from a text, but we have to have the text, and the Prosecution says they don't have the book. So it is quite possible to read a part or a paragraph and ask a question regarding that paragraph, but there's always the problem of context, so perhaps you could prepare your question for a later stage and provide the Prosecution with the appropriate text. But you have already said that you are withdrawing your question, and after these comments, you may proceed, and you can prepare for that question later on if you wish.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the course of the proceedings, the Prosecution will certainly be provided with this document that I referred to just now.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Mr. Butler, are you aware of the fact that in Srebrenica in 1995, there were 6.000 soldiers?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I couldn't claim to give you that number as an exact count, but I would say that that's certainly within the realm of the numbers that I've seen, sir, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: In your examination-in-chief, you said that the column which was partly armed and partly unarmed, that is, consisting of civilians as well, was a legitimate military target.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I recall correctly, in answer to a question by Judge Wald, the answer that I gave was, my understanding of the SFRY application of the Laws of Land Warfare, that under their rules that were applicable, that they would not consider the column -- or that they in fact would consider the column to be a legitimate military target, yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Would it be correct to say when this partly armed column started off towards Jaglici, Bajkovica, Konjevic Polje, Udrc -- no, not Bajkovica, I'm sorry, Ravne Buljim, then across Konjevic Polje towards Udrc, and from there on towards Nezuk, that it was actually engaging in a breakthrough as a combat operation?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is an accurate description of the operation, yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Would it be correct to say that in the minds, though it is difficult to discuss minds as a subjective category, but could it be said that among the military leadership, there must have been awareness that along that route, they would be engaged in combat with the army of Republika Srpska which was holding its static defensive positions?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would say that from the BiH military side and the column, that that would, in fact, be a fair assumption.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: So this cannot be described as a march when it is known that that march has to pass through enemy territory; and when I say "enemy territory," I mean territory under the control of the army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I guess I wouldn't qualify it as certainly an administrative march, and as it was understood by certainly the VRS, again going to your previous description, it was a breakthrough operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: I'm asking you this because during the course of the proceedings, we heard terms such as "march" being used. So along this route, in the course of the breakthrough, if at a certain point in time the two parties engage in combat, the Serb and the Muslim, can anything else be expected but casualties on both sides, at least in the initial stages of that contact or conflict?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Militarily speaking, that's a fair assumption, yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: On that way, through the area -- that is, reaching the area of the Zvornik Brigade, when the head of the column reached the boundary of that area, whereas the end of the column at the same time was south of the communication line Konjevic Polje-Kasaba, the operations that were conducted by the Drina Corps in terms of searching the area, were they legitimate military operations or activities, bearing in mind the fact that it was already evident that the column of the 28th Infantry Division was located in the area? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The sweep operations and the military activity pertaining to engaging the column, as it were, would certainly qualify as military activities. My review of that aspect of the activity, and again, qualifying -- you know, as a lawyer, it's not my place to make a judgement of whether or not it's legitimate or not from a legal sense, but certainly the activities that occurred relevant to the combat engagement of the column fall into a category of normal military activity which one expects. I wouldn't see anything improper or wrong in conducting those military operations.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: The operations in question were, therefore, the ones that were conducted on the 13th and the 14th as well as in the course of the following days, in the area south of the route and also combat activities that had already started in the area of the Zvornik Brigade south of the Konjevic Polje-Kasaba road.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I'm going to object to that, Your Honour. It's not a question. It should be proper. It's also compound and vague as to time and place.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Petrusic, what is your response to the objection?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe that the question was asked in an appropriate manner, especially bearing in mind the fact that we had discussed the issue during the examination-in-chief. I'm referring to the 13th of July, the combat activities and the sweep-up operations that were taking place south of the Konjevic Polje-Kasaba road.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. McCloskey, do you wish to add something to your objection after Mr. Petrusic has responded to it?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. I have no objection to the overall subject matter, certainly. My objection was, as can be read from the question itself, there is no question. It's merely a statement, and he's not even asked to comment on the statement. Not only that, but it's talking about some very serious activity but over a broad range of time and is not specific to the area geographically or -- so he's not even asking Mr. Butler to speculate. It's just an impossible question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is beyond dispute that the issue, the contents of the question, is pertinent. I know that the parties can ask any questions as long as they are relevant and pertinent and relative to the subjects that are discussed, and as long as they're related to the examination-in-chief. But at the same time, we have to have a proper question. If we make assertions, then we will risk the situation of having things in the transcript that need to be further discussed. We really need to have proper questions with a question mark at the end of it. I should like to mention something else as well. We have been hearing this witness for awhile now, and he's an expert witness. Bearing that in mind, it is my opinion that we can discuss his opinions and we can debate his report because we have an expert witness here, and they often testify or give evidence about their opinions and conclusions; however, when we ask an expert witness for an opinion, we have to ask a proper question. So the assertion should be in the form of a question, and we have to avoid compound, composite questions, and we have to avoid posing alternative questions, but we have to go directly to the matter. So, Mr. Petrusic, could you please ask your question in a direct manner, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. When we will show the exhibits to Mr. Butler, I will go back to my previous question, but for the time being, I'm going to withdraw it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Mr. Butler, if the police is under the military command during the combat operations, is it the case that the police continues to be under the military command once the operations in question are completed?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The RS law pertaining to the Ministry of Interior Forces specifically articulates that the police units under military command are under military command for a designated period of time previously agreed by the Ministry of Defence, the Ministry of the Interior, and the President of the Republic, in that context. Having said that, I can't make a blanket statement which says that after the end of a military operation that relationship ceases. If it was the intent of the parties that made the agreement, in which case this is up at the Supreme Command level, that it continue longer, then it would.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: As far as I can understand, you cannot state that that relationship continues after the cessation of the combat activities.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir. What I said is that that relationship continues or ends when it was designated by the authorities that made the relationship. I can't say that the trigger for ending that relationship is the end of combat activities or the end of a certain date. I mean, it's whenever the agreement or whenever the specified organisation and tasking ended.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: The Supreme Command or the Main Staff, do they suggest the use of units to the Ministry of the Interior, that is, the units of the police? Do they merely suggest their use, and is it the Minister of the Interior who makes the final decision as to whether such units will be deployed or not?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, my readings of the pertinent law believe me to understand that the way that the situation works is that the military, in this case, the Main Staff, would request special police support for a determined period and that the Ministry of the Interior, or perhaps even specifically the Minister of the Interior, would make that decision in conjunction with the Minister of Defence and the Supreme Commander of the armed forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: In your report, in your opinion, you speak about the fact that General Major Milenko Zivanovic was replaced or, rather, succeeded by General Major Radislav Krstic, and the date you give for that is the 13th of July.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: When you make this claim, this conclusion, rather, do you take into account the decision of the President of the Republic of the 14th of July whereby it was decided or, rather, decreed by the President of the Republic that the commander of the corps in question would be Radislav Krstic? The decision in question came into force on the 15th of July.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I did take that into account, and I believe I have addressed it in both the written version of the narrative and in my testimony, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: So the Corps Commander, General Major Radislav Krstic, when did he effectively take duty, as of which date? Could you give us the date, please?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Based on my analysis of the information, it is my opinion that General Major Krstic began exercising command of the Drina Corps in the late afternoon, early evening hours of 13 July 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: The only person who was empowered to name, to appoint Corps Commanders, was it the President of the Republic or the Supreme Commander of the armed forces.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Petrusic, I'm sorry, I have to interrupt you once again, but your question had to be who is the person who is empowered to appoint commanders, otherwise you're simply making an assertion with the question mark at the end.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I base myself on the general assumption that it was the President of the Republic, but I do accept your suggestion, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: So, Mr. Butler, who is the person that is empowered to appoint the commander -- Corps Commanders?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Under the relevant laws in question, it would be the President of the Republic, Radovan Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Did the President of the Republic do that in his decree of the 14th of July?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: He, in fact, did that, sir, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Pursuant to that decree, did General Major Radislav Krstic take office on the 15th of July or did the decree in question come into force on the 15th of July?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The decree as written comes into force on 15 July.
