As to the second part of your question, when did General Major Radislav Krstic take office or, in the sense that I infer, begin to exercise command, I would refer back to my earlier answer, that my opinion is he started exercising command on 13 July 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: If we bear in mind the statutory laws regulating the appointment of Corps Commanders, is it true that General Krstic was able to start exercising his function as a Corps Commander in a legitimate and legal manner pursuant to an authorisation by General Mladic?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: If one makes the assumption that General Mladic was, in fact, following an order or directive from the Supreme Commander, then one could in fact do that, in which case General Mladic is essentially operating under the delegated authority of the Supreme Commander to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Which directive do you have in mind when you speak about delegated authority?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not have a specific directive in mind. I base that back under the general principles that subordinates, in their operations, when they give orders and directives, in almost all cases they're giving them under the authority of their superior commander. I have no specific order or directive that designates General Mladic to appoint anyone as a Corps Commander, and specifically under the army law it notes that that authority cannot be delegated from the President. So again, as I noted earlier, if one makes the assumption that General Mladic did, in fact, give this order, the inference has to be that he is giving such an order on the authority of the President of the Republic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: From the documents that were available to you, you could not reach a conclusion as to such powers and authorisations, that is, that the Supreme Commander would transmit such authority to the Commander of the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no information which would indicate that did or did not occur, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Mr. Butler, if the appointment of a Corps Commander is made pursuant to some presidential power, and following the logic -- following that logic, such a presidential power or authority can be delegated, therefore, to vice-presidents and not to the Commander of the Main Staff. Would you agree with that assertion?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, I would have to go back to the original article on the law, but I believe it is extremely specific that that power is vested only with the President. There is no where in my reading of that specific article anything which can be inferred any form of a delegation that can occur. I believe it is extremely specific on that point.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: I accept that the law is very clear in that respect, but I went back to the issue of delegated authority because you actually raised it. As far as I understand you, Mladic was the person who was delegated to appoint General Krstic as a Corps Commander at one point. And I spoke about delegated authority in that context. But I think we understand each other and I can agree that the President of the Republic was the only person who was able to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I should like to suggest a break at this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, this is, indeed, a convenient time for a break. We will have a 20-minute break at this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Petrusic, you may continue. I apologise for the delay. We were here waiting but I think there was a misunderstanding. The break was 20 minutes and not 30 minutes. So having said that, you may continue, Mr. Petrusic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Mr. Butler, we were talking about the regulations governing the appointment of the Corps Commander. My next question is whether you have any information about what is known as the takeover of duty in the army of Republika Srpska, command duties at certain levels, both at the corps level and at the lower echelons, and also in the Main Staff itself?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: My understanding of the process and the documents that I have reflects that that is at the brigade level which reflects a -- or when circumstances allow, a formalised transition of command, or even in respect with a formalised transition of duties, where it's customary that the outgoing person who held those duties, be it a Staff Officer, be it a Chief of Staff, be it a Commander, goes through a briefing process of letting the incoming individual know the status of the unit, where they're going in respect to duties and responsibilities and what the goals are for improving the unit. And then as that transition is done, the incoming officer assumes those duties. I have the document at the brigade level. I assume that the same would hold true for both the Corps and the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: The day of the appointment to a certain position, in this specific case, the appointment by the President of the Republic of General Major Krstic to the position of Corps Commander, is that the same day when the transition is carried out between the outgoing Commander, General Major Zivanovic, and the incoming Commander, in this case General Major Krstic?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: My understanding is that it is not the same day, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: So it must be some later date.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: My understanding is it is, in fact, a later date.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: On the basis --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Excuse me. The answer is which is the later date. I'm sorry. Which takes place after the other. I couldn't understand the answer.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: My understanding is that the actual transition takes place later than --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: After the debriefing.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Excuse me. Later than what?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me try again because I see it on the transcript. The actual -- in the case that we're talking about, the actual transition of command takes place later than the 15 July 1995 date on the order from the President of the Republic. As to a more specific portion, when during Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. that transition phase it takes place, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Excuse me. When you say takes place, do you mean factually, on the ground, or officially?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: When, at a specific point in time in that transition, when there's a document that is signed by the outgoing Commander or the outgoing Staff Officer, the incoming Commander and the incoming Staff Officer, at what point in time in the transition that document is physically signed, and that's what I mean when I say "takes place."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: The documents that you had at your disposal did not include a document on the transition of duty between the outgoing Commander and the incoming Commander who is taking over those duties; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: In view of the fact that a corps can be described as a significant military formation in every sense of the word, that is, that it is composed of quite a number of subordinate brigades with their specific locations, in your opinion, that process of transition or takeover of duty, does it require a minimum of, let me say, ten days for the incoming Commander to become acquainted with the units and everything else he needs to learn about when taking over the duty of Commander?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my army, that would be a fair statement because, for the most part, the Commander is not anyone who has grown up or come through the unit. In this particular instance, I wouldn't say that that would be required when the Commander of the organisation is the former Chief of Staff. There is a presumed detailed working knowledge of the aspects of the corps in this case.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: In your army, Mr. Butler, from the day of the transition of command between the former and the new Commander, does that mark the beginning of the rights and duties of the new Commander and the termination of duties of the former Commander?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the US Army, that process, in all but emergency or sudden circumstances, that transition process occurs prior to the effective date of the order from the superior authority. In rare instances where a Commander is relieved for an unexpected reason, then that transition occurs afterwards. But the customary procedure is that all of the items that are required to be done prior to the assumption of command are accomplished prior to when the effective date of command is designated.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Mr. Butler, from your own experience, was it to be expected -- at the time when the Corps Commander, that is, General Zivanovic, was replaced by General Krstic, were the conditions appropriate for such a replacement to take place just then?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would say that the conditions were not appropriate for the transition process, but the actual replacement or changeover of command doesn't fall into that programme.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Just to remind you, we're talking now about paragraph 15 of your narrative, when you say: "In the confused fighting --" so paragraph 15: "In the confused fighting that follows, the Zvornik Brigade forces were pushed aside and the Muslim column began to envelope the rear areas of three battalions of the Zvornik Brigade."

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, the English language version that I have, the only paragraph 15 is in the executive summary. I believe we have a numbering -- we're out of sequence here from the version you're using and my version.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Just a moment, please. Let me check between the two versions. In the Serbian version, it is page 3, paragraph 15, beginning with the words: "As these first two mass executions are under way, the head of the Muslim column comes into contact with Zvornik Brigade assets."

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay, sir, we're on track.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: "The Muslim forces," or, rather, "column on that occasion began to surround the rear areas of the three battalions of the Zvornik Brigade." How large is that area held by a battalion, in this case holding a defensive posture?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: As indicated on the map, and I believe it's Exhibit 2 which lays out the positions, I mean, coming -- not off of memory, I would say that each battalion held a frontage of between two to three kilometres, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: According to the rules on the structuring of units, is that designated as the area of activity of a battalion?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I presume we're talking the battalion rules at this point, sir. My understanding of those rules is that in the defence, that even for an infantry battalion, that is an extended frontage that is longer than normally doctrine would want it to be.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Could you conclude as to how large a territory it would be in kilometres that was surrounded by the Muslim forces or enveloped?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are we referring to the actual front line positions, or are we referring to a more broader figure which would include the rear zones of the battalion, sir?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: In view of the fact that these three battalions have their own area of operations, their own zones, and that that territory was enveloped or, rather, those battalions were enveloped, can you tell us in kilometres how large that area would be?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I could say it would be a large area. But rather than throw out a figure which could be completely inaccurate, I'd ask for time to do the actual calculations on a map.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Considering that you said that it is a large area, at that point in time, was the Muslim column a serious, a respectable military force in relation to the Zvornik Brigade which was holding a defensive position?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I've testified previously, it certainly represented a significant military threat, even more so because of the fact that it was approaching the battalion defensive positions from the rear in positions where they weren't adequately able to defend themselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: In that conflict, in view of the fact that units of the Zvornik Brigade were holding fortified defensive positions, was it to be expected that there would be considerable losses on the Muslim side, that is, within the moving column?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I've noted in my previous testimony, while the army of the Republika Srpska, the Zvornik Brigade particularly and those battalions specifically, were in fortified positions, it's again worth noting that the fortified positions were facing the main line of confrontation against the forces of the BiH 2nd Corps in the Tuzla area. They were not facing and not geared towards dealing with an enemy column approaching from the south. The quick deployments that were made by the Zvornik Brigade in that respect were immediate deployments to hill or defendable locations; they would not have qualified as fortified areas, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: But the conflict -- an armed conflict did occur, did it not? Or, rather, let me ask you, did an armed conflict occur? Of course, there were casualties on both sides, weren't there?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the context of the military operations that occurred in that area, there were, in fact, casualties on both sides, yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: In the course of your analysis, did you come to learn where the Muslim casualties from that column were buried?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: As part of my analysis, that was one of the questions that I posed to the investigation team which deals with those issues specifically relevant to the crime scene. And what the investigation has revealed was that for the most part, and almost exclusively in that case, that the Muslim casualties that occurred from that column were not, in fact, buried but were left on the surface as surface remains.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: So they were never removed from that area?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: My understanding is that at a point in time after the war, that there were, in fact, some efforts on the part of both the BiH and the Republika Srpska to police up the surface remains in that general area.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Was it not to be expected, Mr. Butler, that an army or a corps and a brigade, such as the Drina Corps and the Zvornik Brigade, to restore the battlefield, precisely what is referred to in the regular, interim, and combat reports by Mr. Pandurevic?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: In respect to the combat operations, and particularly if you intended to occupy the specific ground where that had occurred, it would be reasonable and certainly was mandated within the JNA instructions that the casualties be policed up and disposed of in a sanitary manner, yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: The agreement between the two armies, I'm referring to your previous answer, was this limited to an agreement or were those remains, in fact, policed up from the surface?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, to be honest, I don't know the answer to that question. I know that there was a process involved and I do not know the specifics of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: In the course of your research, did you learn that in that area there were prisoners of war who were sent by the Zvornik Brigade or a superior command to the collection centre or to the camp at Batkovici?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I've discussed in my previous testimony, that at a certain point in time, Muslim prisoners taken by the Zvornik Brigade were, in fact, sent by the brigade and the superior command to the Batkovici collection centre, yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: What's the certain point in time?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe, as I have indicated earlier, based on the daily combat reports of the Zvornik Brigade, the 22nd of July begins the first series of instances where we see that occurring.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: When you say that the first series of instances began on the 22nd of July, was that the date when they were captured or is the 22nd of July the date when they were received and registered by the International Red Cross in the Batkovici camp? So the process of taking prisoners, did that occur prior to the 22nd of July?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: As reflected on the 22 July Zvornik daily combat report, that is the date that they give that they're in the possession of the command of the Zvornik Brigade. I can't speculate as to when they would have been registered by the ICRC at the Batkovici camp, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Do you know, or did you learn in the course of your investigations about the number of prisoners from that area and from the column that were transferred to the camp in Batkovici?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: My understanding, based on the work of the investigation team, is that they have a designated number of individuals who were transferred from the camp who were previously at the Bratunac Medical Centre, and I believe that number is approximately 120. I don't know for sure. I know from my analysis and from dealing with the investigation team that after 22 July, approximately 100 Muslim prisoners, collected over a series of days, were accounted for by the Zvornik Brigade and presumably went to the Batkovici collection centre, but I don't know that. And the only other prisoners that I know that would qualify into the prior category would be the two identified survivors of the Branjevo -- two of the identified survivors of the Branjevo Military Farm massacre who were later taken into custody by, I believe, the Republika Srpska police and later emerged through the camp at Batkovici when the war ended.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: The 10th Sabotage Detachment is a unit of the Main Staff of the army of Republika Srpska, is it not? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Is there any evidence to prove that this unit was subordinated to the Drina Corps at the time when the Commander of the Drina Corps was General Krstic?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no technical evidence that supports that during that period that you've mentioned that the 10th Diversionary Unit was under the command of the Drina Corps, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: We're now talking about the 16th of July and the military farm at Branjevo where executions were carried out by the 10th Diversionist Detachment and the units sent from the Bratunac Brigade. Mr. Butler, can you tell us what that unit consisted of?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which unit, sir, the 10th Diversionary or the unit from the Bratunac Brigade, sir?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: The unit sent from the Bratunac Brigade.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: My understanding, based on the records from the Zvornik and the Bratunac Brigade, is that during that period the unit consisted of two platoons of infantry and, as noted also, a small element of the military police of the Bratunac Brigade who were in Pilica.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: So according to your understanding, at the military farm in Branjevo there were two platoons from the Bratunac Brigade; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir. Two platoons of the Bratunac Brigade were deployed in the Zvornik Brigade area. I do not believe that two full platoons were located in the zone of the -- or in particular at the Branjevo Military Farm that day, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: So at that time they were under the command of the Commander of the Zvornik Brigade, were they?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time the elements of the Bratunac Brigade would have been under the command of the Commander of the Zvornik Brigade, yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: And elements of the military police from Bratunac or, rather, the Bratunac Brigade, when you describe them as elements, could you explain, using military terminology, what you mean when you say "elements"? Do you mean an individual, several individuals, a platoon, a company, a detachment?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe the direct quote from the military police platoon journal during that period comes out in English as "a small portion." I take that to understand, considering the fact that the military police platoon probably numbers approximately 30, that we're talking an element of perhaps five, ten; maybe one vehicle, maybe two. I can't be specific because the actual document isn't specific. I would only assume that they'd have to have their own transportation to get back up there. So I'm qualifying the number as extremely small.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: So we can talk about individuals belonging to the military police, can we?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: In that aspect, I believe it's accurate, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Mr. Butler, you talk about the identification of the Lieutenant Colonel Popovic, Assistant Commander for Security of the Drina Corps, and you mention the date of the 16th of July. You say that he was overseeing the execution process on that date, Lieutenant Colonel Vujadin Popovic.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I make that conclusion. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: On the basis of what? Can you tell us that, please?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The primary documentation that I use would be the series of intercepted telephone communications that discusses the issue in a series of three or four rapid conversations of Colonel Popovic, needing the fuel up at Pilica to finish the job, "job" unspecified; the fact that in the Zvornik Brigade technical records, we have the confirmation that the fuel was, in fact, distributed to him on the dates given in question when he was supposed to be there; the fact that there was no significant military activity up in that area, certainly none which would have required his presence; and the after-the-fact part of the investigation that shows those specific areas would be crime scenes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: So that would be the information on the basis of which you concluded that Popovic was, indeed, on the site of the execution.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the site of the execution and relative to the fuel part of the process, yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, Mr. McCloskey was about to object or ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. McCloskey can respond, but I think that he's just now preparing his redirect examination, no? Mr. McCloskey, did you want to say something?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: No, Mr. President. We're just twitching around over here a bit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, then. Thank you. However, I will take this opportunity to make a short break because we will be working until 2.30 today, and we should split the remaining working time in two parts. We will have a 20-minute break now. We usually have two half-hour breaks which makes one hour, or three 20-minute breaks. Today we decided to have three 20-minute breaks today. This will be our last break today. But it will be only a 20-minute break. [In English] Twenty minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Petrusic, you may continue.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the counsel, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Mr. Butler --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excuse me. We cannot continue because General Krstic is not here yet. Thank you for reminding me.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: There are a few interpreters not in the booth also.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry, Mr. Petrusic, it seems that you can continue now.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Finally. Mr. Butler, considering the type of the Bratunac Brigade, can you tell us whether it had a military police amongst its members?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: By the structure of a former JNA Light Infantry Brigade and that structure adopted by the army of Republika Srpska, military police are not normally found as part of the structure. However, in the case of the Bratunac Brigade, apparently the Commander, of his own volition, organised a group of individuals as a Military Police Platoon to perform the role and functions of military police.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: If we bear that fact in mind, could you tell us who it was who would put the military police in question in use?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The technical aspect of overseeing the functions of the military police would fall under the purview of the brigade Assistant Commander for Security and Intelligence. The command of the police platoon would be exercised by the Brigade Commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Would that constitute also a legal aspect of the use of the military police?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: In that regard, I'm not qualified to answer the question, sir. I don't know and would not know if whether or not the organisation of the Military Police Platoon is structured, authorise them to have the bona fide military police and law enforcement roles and aspects in question. My assumption is that it would because the organisation was bona fide by the Brigade Commander, but again I can't answer that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Mr. Butler, considering the material that was available to you and relating to the Bratunac Brigade, did you come across a piece of evidence which would indicate that Lieutenant Colonel Blagojevic put into use a certain number of policemen from that particular platoon, that is, the Military Police Platoon, on the 16th of July?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I have is from the 16th of July the journal that notes what the police are doing. I cannot specifically say that Colonel Blagojevic directly and specifically ordered them to do those functions.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Was it possible that this was ordered to them by someone else?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I indicated earlier, the role of overseeing the military police would have fallen under the purview of the Brigade Assistant Commander for Intelligence and Security, and either further down in the command chain, the Military Police Platoon Commander could have ordered them to do this as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: I have to go back to one of your previous questions, Mr. Butler. You said you had the journal of the military police or the journal of the platoon. I don't think I understood you correctly. What kind of journal did you have in mind? Whose journal was it?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the -- and perhaps "journal" is an inaccurate word. This is a logbook that shows the daily activities of the Military Police Platoon of the Bratunac Light Infantry Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: In the rules and regulations relating to the land army in peacetime, talking about the security body, Article 29 --

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a second, Mr. President. Mr. Visnjic has helped me. This is the additional material relating to the report on the command responsibility, footnote number 10. The issue discussed is the role of the security body, Article 29, paragraph 9 -- Article 29, paragraph 9 -- where it is stated as follows -- we can put it on the ELMO if the Chamber deems it necessary or if it will be of assistance to Mr. Butler.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Could you please turn to the next page, paragraph 9, please. The passage reads as follows: "Expertly directing security organs and the military police in the corps command and units and in other JNA units in the zone of responsibility, organising, directing and coordinating their activities, providing assistance and controlling their work, especially in regard to counter-intelligence work and tasks." Mr. Butler, does that mean that the Security Organ can use the military police belonging to the Bratunac Brigade?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I can clarify your question. Are you referring to can the corps Security Organ ...

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: My reading of that would be that while they can technically manage that, the actual usage of the military police would be contingent upon the approval of the echelons commander, which would mean that presumably for the corps to request the use of the police to do that, the Corps Commander would have to either order that to occur or the subordinate Brigade Commander would have to receive that in the form of a request from the corps security officer, approve it, and to make his unit available for their use. Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: The rule pertaining to the security organs of the armed forces of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia of 1984 states as follows --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone to the counsel, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Could we get an exhibit number or some reference so we can know where to go to find what counsel is referring to?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, we need one second for this. I'm sorry for this interruption. It is within the same documents as the previous quotation and it can be found in footnote 34.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Is that enough for you, Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, I think we've got that document. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If the Chamber thinks it is necessary, we can put the material in question on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: No, really, it is not necessary. You can continue, Mr. Petrusic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 16, the following is stated: "The Security Organ is subordinate to the commanding officer of the command, unit, institution or staff of the armed forces in whose strength it is placed in the establishment, and it is responsible to that officer for its work, while JNA security organs in organisations for NVO are responsible to the competent Assistant Federal Secretary for National Defence." In paragraph 18, it is stated as follows: "The security organs of the superior command, unit, institution, or staff of the armed forces provide and they are --"

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, but the interpreters do not have the relevant text.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry, Mr. Petrusic, but the interpreters are telling me that they do need the text on the ELMO. I have to change my previous decision. So if we can please have it on the ELMO now. Yes, Mr. Petrusic, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: I am referring to paragraph 18, and I will repeat: "The security organs of the superior command, unit, institution, or staff of the armed forces provide specialist administrative services for security organs in subordinate commands, units, institutions, and staffs of the armed forces, provide assistance to these organs, and organise, direct, coordinate, and supervise their work." In relation to the same issue, we have one additional rule, that is, one additional paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I can have the assistance of the usher, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Paragraph 49 states in its second passage the following: "An officer, under paragraph 1 of this item," which we have discussed, "may pass on information that constitutes an official secret to other authorised Security Organ officers or other persons only with the authorisation of his superior officer in the Security Organ." Mr. Butler, does this mean that the Corps Commander could not -- that is, his Assistant Commander for Security was not under the obligation to inform him about the usage of the military police?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir, I wouldn't interpret that at all. I would refer back to the base paragraph which starts the programme, paragraph 16, placing the Security Organ directly subordinate to the commanding officer of the commanding unit. The Security Organ manages the military police. Under the theory that you've surfaced, what that means is that the Security Organ of a superior Command can bypass a subordinate Brigade Commander, in effect bypass the subordinate Brigade Assistant Commander for Security and Intelligence and directly task the military police. And I don't believe that that's a militarily realistic scenario under the regulations as stated, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: I could agree with you regarding paragraph 16. But paragraph 49 of those same rules excludes the Corps Commander -- whereas the Commander for Security and Intelligence of the Main Staff, without giving the Assistant Commander for Security to inform his Corps Commander about certain activities. I think that in this paragraph, paragraph 49, this is explicitly stated.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I disagree, sir. I don't share that interpretation at all, particularly the phrase "and other persons" or "other persons." With this regard, and again based on the theory that you've advanced, even in a circumstance where that could occur classified as a secret, somebody has to inform the Brigade Commander that his military police or elements of his units are being taken away from him. They cannot just disappear in isolation and not let anyone know where they're going or what they're doing.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Is the Assistant Commander for Security authorised to take that unit and use it, according to Article 29 [as interpreted], point 9, of the Rules on the Authority of the Corps Command?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could I ask you to show me that particular passage, please. I don't seem to have it in front of me.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: This abstract was under the ELMO a moment ago.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: My apologies. I thought you were referring to a different -- could you restate the question again, sir, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excuse me for interrupting. We are talking about paragraph 49, are we not? Because I see in the transcript it mentions Article 29, point 9, and on the ELMO I can see that we're looking at Article 49.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The question relates to Article 29 of the Rules on the Authority of the Ground Forces Corps Commander, which was previously on the ELMO, Article 29 of those regulations.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not have those rules in front of me, sir, no. I'm sorry. I believe -- here we go. I believe this is what we're referring to, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is it precisely.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Page 2, please, point 9. So my question is: Can the Security Organ commit the use of the military police? Can the Security Organ, the Assistant Commander for Security, deploy the military police?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: And we're discussing this in the context of the Corps Assistant Commander for Security deploy the subordinate brigade military police; correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Yes, precisely. I thought we cleared that point up at the beginning.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I just want to make sure that it didn't change, sir. In that respect, I would say no, sir, because when one looks at the functions of the Security Organ at the superior unit as well as the Security Organ at that level, in both cases it specifically notes that it is the function of the Assistant Commander for Security to advise the Commander on the uses of the military police; to be able, on one hand, to say that the Assistant Commander for Security and Intelligence -- or Security, in this case, at the Corps, who has to advise the Commander and recommend courses of action for the Corps military police, can in and of his own volition pass the military police of a subordinate brigade without informing either the Brigade Commander or the Brigade Assistant Commander for Security and Intelligence doesn't make logical sense, sir. And because of that, I would disagree with your statement, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Mr. Butler, that is not what I am claiming. I was just quoting from a legal provision of these rules. To conclude with that, your opinion disowns or refutes this Article 29 or, rather, paragraph 9 of Article 29.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir, that's not correct. What I am saying is that when you read the series of the regulations and the articles in their totality, in an entire context, it becomes clear that the role of the Assistant Commander for Security at both the Corps and at the Brigade echelon is to determine tasks and uses for the military police and to propose them for the adoption of the relevant Commanders. It is within that entire context that I make the conclusion that it is not militarily sound or feasible that a superior Assistant Commander would reach down to a subordinate unit and do that in isolation. So based on my total analysis of all the material relevant to these regulations, that's where I make my conclusion.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: If the Assistant Commander for Security of the corps orders the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. use of the police, the Assistant Commander for Security and Intelligence of the Main Staff, would you still maintain your opinion that the Assistant Commander for Security at the corps level would be obliged to advise the Corps Commander about it?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, if you just wait for a second. That was a long question and I want to read the whole transcript before I answer. Okay. I'm afraid I'm confused with the question, sir. Could I ask you to restate it, please. It doesn't make sense to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: If the Assistant Commander for Security at the corps level receives an order on the use of the military police from the Assistant Commander for Security and Intelligence Affairs of the Main Staff, would the Assistant Corps Commander for Security in that case be obliged to advise the Corps Commander of the same in that case?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Now I understand, sir. In that regard, if the Assistant Commander of the corps received instructions pertaining to the use of the military police, and considering that the military police are subordinate to the Corps Commander, the Assistant Commander for Security of the corps should inform the Commander as to what the utilisation instructions are. He should be informed of that, yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Mr. Butler, your opinion and the formal regulations governing the competencies of the Corps Command and the Security and Intelligence Service regulations differ substantively. But in any event, I will not have any more questions for you in this regard.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I beg you for your indulgence, Mr. President, for a moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Mr. Butler, we're going back to your report, when you're speaking about the engagement of Colonel Slobodan Cerovic and the intercept of the conversation between Cerovic and Beara. My question is: If triage, which is the subject of that conversation, can be defined as an operation which may mean separation of the wounded from the fit or separation of the more seriously wounded from the lightly wounded, could the word "triage" or the concept of triage also mean separation of military-aged, armed men from unarmed, or women and children from the men who are fit for military service? Generally, can this term have multifold meanings in a broader context?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: In fairness, sir, the military lexicon defines the term in a medical sense. I would hesitate to get very far down the road speculating what the phrase "triage" might mean in various other forms of potentially criminal or noncriminal applications. It is the word that they used, and, as I generally note, I try not to put additional or more meaning into their words than is self-evident.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: I'm sorry. What do you mean by "self-evident"?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, they use the phrase "triage." One possible explanation is, as Mr. Petrusic forwards, there could be multiple possibly explanations. All I'm saying as part of my analysis is here's the word that was used, as translated, and I would prefer not to try to speculate as to what they really mean behind that individual word, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: So it's not self-evident.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Agreed, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Mr. Butler, this word, "triage," do you use it exclusively in the way defined in the dictionary?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Do I use it personally in a military sense or in an individual sense, sir?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: In your report.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Triage, as described and in my report, I believe, refers to a separation process, but I'm not specific as to who the separation process is. I use "triage" in the report, again, as a quotation of what the translation notes. If you could direct me to a specific paragraph in question, maybe I can clarify it further for you in that regard, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: That is quite sufficient. It is the word used in the conversation between Colonel Cerovic and Beara.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I would suggest we adjourn for today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Petrusic, we're going to accept your suggestion. It is most appropriate. We've come to the end of our work for today, and we will meet here again tomorrow at 9.30 to continue the hearing. Thank you very much, and have a good afternoon, all of you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 20th day of July, 2000, at 9.30 a.m. 24 25
